W1. Foundations of Probability

Author

Ramil Nasibullin

Published

September 10, 2026

1. Theory

1.1 Random Experiments, Outcomes, and Sample Spaces

A random experiment is any repeatable physical observation, measurement, or procedure whose outcome cannot be predicted with absolute certainty in advance, but whose set of all conceivable results can be fully cataloged before execution.

An individual, indivisible result of a single realization of a random experiment is called an elementary outcome (or sample point), denoted by . The collection of all possible elementary outcomes forms the universal set of the experiment, termed the sample space, denoted by (or ). Every performance of the experiment terminates in precisely one outcome . The outcomes comprising must be:

  1. Mutually exclusive: No two distinct outcomes () can occur simultaneously on a single trial.
  2. Collectively exhaustive: At least one outcome must occur whenever the experiment is performed.
1.1.1 Why Formalizing the Sample Space Matters

In probability theory, probabilities cannot be assigned in an abstract void; they are defined strictly as set functions over subsets of a predetermined reference universe. Choosing and precisely specifying defines the universe of discourse. An ambiguous, incomplete, or ill-defined sample space undermines the subsequent assignment of probabilities, leading directly to logical paradoxes and invalid normalizations.

1.1.2 Classification of Sample Spaces by Cardinality

The mathematical structure of a probability model depends fundamentally on the cardinality of the sample space:

  1. Finite Sample Spaces (): The set contains a finite number of discrete elements.
    • Tossing a single coin: , with .
    • Rolling a standard six-sided die: , with .
    • Tossing a coin three consecutive times:
  2. Countably Infinite Sample Spaces (): The outcomes can be arranged in an infinite sequence and placed in a one-to-one correspondence with the non-negative integers .
    • Network traffic monitoring: Counting the total number of email packets arriving at a mail server within a fixed one-hour window:
    • Repeated trials until success: Tossing a coin repeatedly until the first Head appears, recording the total number of tosses required: .
  3. Uncountably Infinite (Continuous) Sample Spaces (): The outcomes form a continuum and cannot be listed or indexed by the integers; they represent intervals or regions in Euclidean space .
    • Component reliability: The operational lifespan of an electronic component until failure:
    • Analog electrical measurements: The instantaneous voltage across a noisy resistor: .
    • Thermodynamic tracking: A continuous temperature measurement: (or on the Kelvin scale).
    • Particle physics: The exact spatial coordinates of a subatomic particle inside a reaction chamber: .
    • Signal sampling: The exact arrival time (in milliseconds) of an atmospheric static electrical pulse captured by a radio receiver.
1.1.3 The Granularity Principle

A physical experiment does not possess a uniquely mandated mathematical sample space. The choice of is an abstraction dictated entirely by the observer’s engineering or experimental objectives. The same physical trial can be described by sample spaces of differing granularity:

Consider rolling a standard six-sided die:

  • If the objective is to observe the exact face that lands upward:
  • If the objective is only to record the parity of the score:

Sample space has finer granularity than . It provides strictly more information: knowledge of an outcome in uniquely determines the corresponding outcome in (e.g., observing immediately implies the outcome is ). Conversely, observing does not reveal whether the true face in was or . The macro-outcomes of correspond to a non-overlapping partition of the micro-outcomes of :

An automated test station evaluates two microchips off an assembly line sequentially. Each chip is classified either as passing () or defective ().

  1. Detailed Sample Space (Order-Preserving): If the technician tracks the individual identity and order of the chips:

The mapping between the granular spaces maps , , and . Both formulations are mathematically valid descriptions of the experiment, but is required if one needs to determine whether the first chip specifically was defective.

1.1.5 Common Pitfalls
  • Confusing Outcomes with Events: An outcome is an indivisible element of the set (). An event is a subset of (). While a singleton set contains only one outcome, it is formally an event, not an outcome: .
  • Violating Mutual Exclusivity: Constructing candidate sample spaces whose elements overlap. For instance, proposing for a single die roll fails because the roll is simultaneously even and prime, violating the requirement that exactly one element of occurs per trial.
  • Assuming Uniform Likelihood on Coarse Spaces: Coarse spaces constructed by aggregating granular outcomes do not inherit uniform probabilities. In the microchip illustration, even if each chip in has an equal chance of passing or failing (making all 4 sequence outcomes equally likely with probability ), the elements in are not equally likely: outcome corresponds to and thus has twice the probability of outcome () or outcome ().
1.2 Events, Set Operations, and Algebraic Identities

An event is a subset of the sample space (written ). We say that the event occurs in a trial of a random experiment if the realized outcome is an element of , that is, . The collection of all observable events is denoted by . Events are classified according to their structure and cardinality:

  • An elementary event (or simple event) consists of a single individual outcome: a singleton set .
  • A compound event contains two or more distinct outcomes, formed by grouping elementary outcomes together (for example, rolling an even number on a six-sided die: ).
  • The certain event is the entire sample space itself. Because every valid trial produces some outcome , the certain event occurs inevitably in every execution of the experiment.
  • The impossible event (or null event) is the empty set (also denoted ). It contains no sample points; hence, it can never occur.
1.2.1 Why Event Formalism Matters

Translating experimental hypotheses into set-theoretic structures replaces informal verbal statements with unambiguous mathematical objects. When events are formalized as subsets of , probabilistic questions about combinations of occurrences (“both happen”, “at least one happens”, “neither happens”) translate directly into rigorous operations of Boolean algebra.

1.2.2 Event Operations and Set Relations

Let and be two events associated with the same sample space . New events are generated through standard set operations:

  • Complement: The complement of an event with respect to , denoted by (or ), is the set of all outcomes in that do not belong to : represents the event that does not occur.
  • Intersection: The intersection of two events and , denoted , is the event containing all outcomes that belong simultaneously to both and : represents the joint occurrence of both and .
  • Union: The union of two events and , denoted , is the event containing all outcomes that belong to , to , or to both: represents the occurrence of at least one of the two events.
  • Set Difference: The difference of event and event , denoted , is the set of outcomes belonging to but not to : represents the event that occurs while fails to occur.
  • Mutual Exclusivity: Two events and are mutually exclusive (or disjoint) if they share no outcomes: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur simultaneously in a single trial.

1.2.6 Common Pitfalls
  • Mutually Exclusive vs. Independent: Mutual exclusivity is a purely set-theoretic property (: the sets do not overlap). Independence is a probabilistic property (). Two non-empty events with non-zero probability can never be both mutually exclusive and independent.
  • The Empty Set vs. : The empty set contains no elements whatsoever (). In contrast, is a valid non-empty elementary event containing the numerical outcome (for instance, receiving zero errors on an interface).
  • Asymmetry of Set Difference: Unlike union and intersection, set difference is non-commutative: in general. represents “ occurs and does not”, whereas represents “ occurs and does not”.
1.3 Empirical and Classical Models of Probability

The bridge between physical observation and abstract mathematical modeling is established through two foundational frameworks: the empirical model based on observed frequencies and the classical model based on physical symmetry.

1.3.1 Empirical Probability and the Frequency Stabilization Principle

The empirical probability (or relative frequency probability) of an event approximates its likelihood of occurrence via empirical observation. Suppose an experiment is repeated independently times under identical conditions. If event occurs in exactly of these trials, the relative frequency is defined as:

The empirical probability assigns:

The operational validity of this definition rests on the empirical observation known as the frequency stabilization principle: as the number of independent trials grows arbitrarily large (), the relative frequency ceases to fluctuate erratically and stabilizes around a distinct, constant numerical value :

1.3.2 The Classical (Laplace) Probability Model

While the empirical model operates a posteriori (after collecting data), the classical definition of probability operates a priori by deducing probabilities from the geometric or physical symmetries of the experiment.

Let be a finite sample space containing mutually exclusive elementary outcomes: . If all elementary outcomes are equally likely (equiprobable) due to physical symmetry, then each outcome must carry identical probability mass:

For any compound event consisting of favorable outcomes, the classical probability of is the ratio of the cardinality of to the cardinality of :

1.3.4 Limitations and Common Pitfalls

Both models possess structural limitations that prevent them from serving as universal mathematical foundations:

  • Limitations of the Empirical Model: It requires experiments that are infinitely and independently repeatable under invariant physical conditions. Phenomena that are singular, unique (e.g., forecasting the probability of an unprecedented geopolitical or macroeconomic event), or non-stationary cannot be evaluated empirically. Furthermore, for any finite , yields only an empirical estimate, never the exact theoretical probability.
  • Limitations of the Classical Model: It strictly requires a finite sample space and hinges upon the assumption of equiprobability. Assuming equal likelihood in systems lacking physical symmetry leads to fallacious conclusions.
  • Common Pitfall — Circular Reasoning: Defining classical probability as the ratio of favorable to total outcomes when all outcomes are equally likely is inherently circular: “equally likely” means having “equal probability,” using the concept of probability to define probability itself. This circularity necessitated Kolmogorov’s axiomatic formulation.
1.4 Discrete Probability Spaces with Non-Uniform Weights

The classical probability model assumes that all elementary outcomes are equally likely, assigning an identical mass to each sample point. However, real-world physical systems frequently exhibit structural imbalances, manufacturing asymmetries, or heterogeneous frequencies. To accommodate these scenarios, probability theory generalizes discrete models by assigning an individual non-negative parameter—termed an outcome weight or elementary probability—to each individual point in the sample space.

Let be a finite or countably infinite sample space. An elementary probability assignment (or weight function) is a mapping associating each elementary outcome with a real weight such that:

  1. Non-negativity: Every outcome weight is non-negative:
  2. Total Probability Weight Condition (Normalization): The aggregate weight of all mutually exclusive elementary outcomes in the universe equals unity:

For any arbitrary compound event , the probability of an event under this weighted measure is defined by the discrete aggregation of the weights of all sample points comprising :

By construction, this formulation naturally guarantees , , and , aligning directly with finite and countable additivity over disjoint elementary singletons.

1.5 Geometric Probability on Continuous Domains

When a random experiment generates outcomes from an uncountably infinite set, the classical discrete ratio becomes mathematically undefined because , while individual singleton outcomes have probability zero. Geometric probability resolves this limitation by extending the principle of equally likely outcomes to continuous domains through geometric measure.

Let the sample space be a measurable subset of Euclidean space with a finite, strictly positive -dimensional Lebesgue measure . If an outcome is chosen uniformly at random from —meaning the probability of an outcome landing inside an event region depends strictly on its size and is invariant under spatial translations within —the geometric probability of an event is defined as the ratio:

  • Length () when ,

Because geometric probability maps subsets of Euclidean space to numbers in via ratios of standard measures, analyzing events reduces to setting up coordinate spaces, translating probabilistic conditions into systems of inequalities, and computing bounding geometries.

1.5.3 Pitfalls in Geometric Probability
  1. Equating Probability Zero with Impossibility:
    In discrete probability, . In continuous geometric probability, any lower-dimensional subset has measure zero. The event that Alice and Bob arrive at the exact same millisecond () corresponds to the diagonal line segment of length in . Because the area of a line in is 0, , even though simultaneous arrival is physically possible.
  2. Failure of the Uniformity Assumption:
    The geometric ratio is valid only if the random variable is uniformly distributed over the coordinates defining the domain. If arrival times cluster around peak commuter hours, the probability mass is no longer proportional to Euclidean area, requiring weighted bivariate integration () rather than simple geometric ratios.
1.6 Sigma-Algebras and Measurable Spaces

In discrete models with finite sample spaces , every subset can be assigned an unambiguous probability by summing the weights of its individual outcomes: the event space is simply the power set . However, when the sample space is uncountably infinite (such as the real line or the unit interval ), defining a uniform, translation-invariant probability measure on the entire power set is mathematically impossible. Vitali’s theorem demonstrates that assuming the Axiom of Choice yields non-measurable subsets for which no probability can be assigned without violating countable additivity. To prevent such paradoxes, probability measures are defined on a restricted, well-behaved collection of subsets called a -algebra.

1.6.1 Axiomatic Definition and Measurable Spaces

Let be a non-empty set representing the sample space. A collection of subsets of is called a -algebra (or -field) on if it satisfies three axioms:

  1. Contains the Universal Set:
  2. Closure under Complements:
  3. Closure under Countable Unions:

The ordered pair is called a measurable space. The sets are called measurable sets; in the context of probability theory, they constitute the allowable events to which probabilities can be assigned.

From these axioms, several immediate structural properties follow:

  • Contains the Empty Set: Setting , Axiom 2 guarantees that .
  • Closure under Finite Unions: Any finite sequence can be extended into a countable sequence by setting for all . Hence, .
  • Closure under Countable Intersections: By De Morgan’s laws: Since each , their countable union lies in , and the complement of that union also belongs to .
1.6.2 Catalog of Fundamental -Algebras

Depending on the resolution of information required, different -algebras can be constructed on the same underlying set :

  • Trivial (Minimal) -Algebra: This represents the state of complete lack of information: one can only determine whether an outcome occurs within (certain event) or outside it (impossible event).
  • Power Set (Maximal) -Algebra: Contains every subset of . For any finite set of size , the power set contains exactly events.
  • -Algebra Generated by a Single Event: For any proper, non-empty subset , the smallest -algebra containing is:
  • -Algebra Generated by a Finite Partition: Let be a partition of into pairwise disjoint, non-empty subsets such that . The sets act as indivisible building blocks called atoms. The smallest -algebra containing all , denoted , consists of all possible unions of these atoms (including the empty union ). The total number of elements in this generated -algebra is:

1.6.4 Continuous and Infinite Structures

When is continuous or uncountable, discrete partition techniques do not suffice:

  • Borel -Algebra on : The standard measurable space on the real line is , where the Borel -algebra is the -algebra generated by all open intervals: Because is closed under countable intersections and complements, it automatically contains:

    • Closed intervals:
    • Semi-open intervals:
    • Singletons:
    • Countable sets such as the rationals

  • Countable-Cocountable -Algebra: For an arbitrary uncountable set , the collection: forms a valid -algebra. If are all countable, their union is countable. If at least one has a countable complement , then is a subset of a countable set, hence countable.

1.6.5 Common Pitfalls
  • Confusing Finite Additivity with Countable Additivity: A collection closed only under finite unions and complements is called an algebra (or field) of sets. A -algebra requires closure under countable (infinitely enumerable) unions. On finite sets, every algebra is trivially a -algebra because finite sets have only finitely many subsets; on infinite sets, an algebra is not necessarily a -algebra.
  • Testing Membership of Outcomes vs. Subsets: A -algebra is a family of subsets, not a set of elementary outcomes. If , the element is not in ; rather, the singleton may or may not belong to .

Understanding how collections of measurable sets behave under these algebraic operations is essential for constructing complex measurable spaces, defining generated -algebras, and establishing the limits of combining information structures.

1.8 Kolmogorov Axioms and Probability Spaces

The modern mathematical foundation of probability theory, formulated by Andrey Kolmogorov in 1933, establishes probability as an axiomatic measure on an event space.

Let be a sample space and be a -algebra of events defined on , forming the measurable space . A probability measure is a real-valued set function that maps each event to a real number while satisfying three fundamental postulates, known as the Kolmogorov axioms:

  1. Axiom 1 (Non-negativity): For every event , Probabilities are non-negative real numbers; negative likelihoods are physically and mathematically impermissible.
  2. Axiom 2 (Normalization): For the universal event , The random experiment is guaranteed to yield an outcome within the sample space. The total probability mass across the entire system is exactly unity.
  3. Axiom 3 (Countable Additivity / -Additivity): For any countable sequence of pairwise disjoint (mutually exclusive) events (where for all ),

The mathematical structure combining the sample space, the event -algebra, and the probability measure is called a probability space.

1.8.1 Motivation and Conceptual Role

The axiomatic definition replaces earlier intuitive or heuristic paradigms—such as naive classical ratio counting or purely empirical long-run frequencies—with a rigorous, self-consistent mathematical framework. It guarantees that calculations across finite, countably infinite, and continuous spaces behave consistently without encountering paradoxes, while naturally accommodating the measure-theoretic architecture needed for advanced calculus and stochastic processes.

1.8.5 Pitfalls and Misconceptions
  • Confusing the Domain of : A probability measure is defined on events (elements of the -algebra ), never directly on raw outcomes unless wrapped as singletons . Writing instead of conflates an element with a set.
  • Assuming Boundedness Implies Additivity: A function satisfying and is not necessarily a probability measure. Non-linear functions of set sizes or geometric boundaries routinely fail additivity.
  • Conflating Finite and Countable Additivity: Finite additivity ( for disjoint ) is strictly weaker than countable additivity (-additivity). Countable additivity is required to guarantee continuity properties of measures on infinite spaces and limit theorems for infinite sequences of events.
1.9 Fundamental Consequences of the Kolmogorov Axioms

The Kolmogorov axioms define a minimal, non-redundant set of rules governing a probability measure on a measurable space . Every operational theorem of probability theory descends directly from these three core statements: non-negativity (), normalization (), and countable additivity ( for mutually disjoint sets).

Establishing the fundamental consequences of these axioms guarantees that the probability measure behaves consistently with intuitive notions of proportions, boundaries, and set operations without introducing extraneous assumptions.

1.10 Addition Rules and the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion

Kolmogorov’s third axiom defines additivity strictly for pairwise disjoint collections of events. When events overlap, simply summing their individual probabilities overcounts the probability mass residing within their intersections. The addition rule and its generalization, the principle of inclusion-exclusion, provide the exact analytical framework required to compute the probability of unions and composite configurations for arbitrary, non-disjoint events.

2. Definitions

  • Random Experiment: A process or observational procedure whose exact outcome cannot be predicted with certainty in advance, but whose set of all possible outcomes is fully specifiable.
  • Sample Space: The set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment, conventionally denoted by or .
  • Outcome: A single, specific elementary result obtained from a single performance of a random experiment.
  • Event: Any subset of a sample space whose occurrence is identified with the realized outcome belonging to that subset.
  • Simple Event: An event consisting of exactly one individual outcome from the sample space.
  • Compound Event: An event containing two or more distinct outcomes from the sample space.
  • Certain Event: The event corresponding to the entire sample space , which is guaranteed to occur on every trial of an experiment.
  • Null Event (Impossible Event): The empty set , representing an event that contains no outcomes and therefore can never occur.
  • Complement of an Event: The event denoted or consisting of all outcomes in the sample space that do not belong to , occurring if and only if does not occur.
  • Intersection of Events: The event denoted comprising all outcomes belonging simultaneously to both and , which occurs if and only if both events occur.
  • Union of Events: The event denoted comprising all outcomes belonging to , to , or to both, which occurs if and only if at least one of the events occurs.
  • Mutually Exclusive (Disjoint) Events: Two or more events that share no common outcomes (), precluding their simultaneous occurrence in a single experimental trial.
  • Empirical Probability: The probability assigned to an event defined as the limiting relative frequency of its occurrence over an infinite sequence of identical and independent trials.
  • Classical Probability: The probability framework defined on a finite sample space of equally likely elementary outcomes, where the probability of an event equals the ratio of the number of favorable outcomes to the total number of possible outcomes.
  • Geometric Probability: An extension of the classical definition to continuous spaces where the probability of an event is the ratio of its geometric measure (length, area, or volume) to the total measure of the bounded sample space.
  • -Algebra: A collection of subsets of a sample space that contains and is closed under complementation and countable unions.
  • Measurable Space: A mathematical pair consisting of a non-empty sample space equipped with a designated -algebra of admissible events.
  • Probability Measure: A real-valued function defined on a -algebra that satisfies non-negativity (), normalization (), and countable additivity across mutually disjoint sequences of events.
  • Probability Space: The formal Kolmogorov axiomatic triple completely characterizing a random phenomenon by specifying its sample space, the -algebra of observable events, and the assigned probability measure.
  • Atom: A non-empty event in a -algebra that contains no other proper non-empty sub-events belonging to that -algebra, acting as an indivisible structural component of the event space.
